captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 7. In this lesson: The audition.
Read a play script and understand how dialogue shows character.
Here are some new words. Audition. A short performance to get a part in a play. Director.
The person who tells the actors what to do. Rehearsal. A practice of a play before the real show.
And some more words. Stage fright. Fear of performing in front of people. Monologue.
A long speech by one character. Cue. A word or action that tells an actor to start.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: a short performance to get a part in a play?
Now some grammar: Reporting verbs. Choose reporting verbs that show how something is said: insisted,
admitted, suggested, complained, explained, warned. For example: ‘I didn't do it,’ he insisted.
For example: ‘I'm a bit nervous,’ she admitted.
Now listen, and read along. The audition. (A school hall. Ms Aria, the director, sits with a clipboard.
Tom waits nervously at the side of the stage.) Ms Aria: Next! Tom Riley, please.
Tom: (stepping forward slowly) Um… I'm not sure I can do this. Ms Aria: (kindly) Stage fright is normal.
Take a deep breath. When you're ready, start your monologue. Tom: (breathes in,
then speaks loudly and clearly) ‘I am the captain of this ship, and I will not let it sink!’ (Silence.
Then Ms Aria puts down her pen.)
Ms Aria: Tom, that was the best audition I've heard today. Rehearsals start on Monday.
Tom: (amazed, then grinning) Really? Thank you!
Another question. The video will stop. Where does the scene take place?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like audition, director, rehearsal. You practised reporting verbs.
And you read The audition. Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

sections.title: Writing dialogue

q.prompt: Which word means “a conversation between characters”?

options.fb: “sarcastic” means saying the opposite of what you mean to be unkind or funny.
“tone” means the feeling in someone's voice.

captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 7. In this lesson: Writing dialogue.
Punctuate dialogue correctly and use adverbs to show tone.
Here are some new words. Dialogue. A conversation between characters. Tone. The feeling in someone's voice.
Sarcastic. Saying the opposite of what you mean to be unkind or funny.
And some more words. Hesitantly. Slowly, because you are not sure. Interrupt.
Start speaking while someone else is speaking. Reluctantly. Not wanting to do something.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: a conversation between characters?
Now some grammar: Punctuating dialogue. Start a new line for each new speaker.
Put punctuation inside the speech marks. If the speech is split, use a comma and a small letter to continue.
For example: ‘I think,’ she said slowly, ‘we should go back.’ For example: ‘Stop!’ shouted Dad.
Now listen, and read along. The broken vase.
‘Who broke the vase?’ asked Mum, staring at the pieces on the floor. ‘It wasn't me,’ said Jamal quickly.
‘It wasn't me either,’ said his sister Hana. Then she added sarcastically,
‘Maybe the cat learned to play football.’ Jamal looked at the ball under the sofa.
‘Well,’ he began hesitantly, ‘I might have been practising my kicks…
a little bit.’ ‘In the living room?’ Mum interrupted. ‘Only once,’ Jamal said, reluctantly. ‘I'm sorry.
I'll buy you a new one with my pocket money.’
Mum sighed, but a small smile appeared on her face. ‘Next time,’ she said, ‘practise in the garden.’
Another question. The video will stop. What was broken?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like dialogue, tone, sarcastic. You practised punctuating dialogue.
And you read The broken vase. Now try the practice questions. See you next time!
